svg.aria-label: Density stratification and the foam limit
svg.title: Density stratification and the foam limit
svg.desc: Densities 1.15 > 1.01 > 0.35 give stable layers; foam damage is observed at 0.022% yolk contamination.
svg.text: Stratification is arithmetic, not luck — and the foam's real enemy is not gravity but a trace of yolk.
Each layer is denser than the one above it, by a wide margin. Pour gently and the
order is thermodynamically expected rather than a trick of technique.
yolk in the white is the most sensitive point in the published
evidence at which foam damage has been OBSERVED.
That is roughly a single drop of yolk in a cup of white. So the
requirement is not "be careful" but zero deliberate yolk carryover.
This is why the two halves are built in separate bowls and never whisked together: yolk lipid and LDL outcompete albumen
at the air-water interface and collapse the foam.
The number is a floor on the EVIDENCE, not a proven safe threshold — nothing here shows that 0.022% is harmless,
only that damage has been observed at it.
